title: Back to the future: Architect Lord Norman Foster revisits our Hong Kong HQ
summary: Lord Norman Foster, architect of HSBC’s Hong Kong HQ, returns 40 years after it opened – and reflects on how its “radical” concept inspired future developments.
body_markdown:
Since 1986, our main building at 1 Queen’s Road Central, in Hong Kong, has been an eye-catching landmark on the city’s skyline. Forty years after the building he designed opened, architect Lord Norman Foster, who is now 92, came back for an anniversary tour.


In his own words below, he explains how the building’s construction challenged the traditional office building concept and was a beacon for the future.


‘There is nothing like this building’


(duration 3:35)


Architect Lord Norman Foster returns to our HQ in Hong Kong to mark its 40th anniversary


### Norman Foster interview at 1QRC


**Duration:** 3:35


**Speakers:**


- Lord Norman Foster, Architect
[LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/in/norman-foster-760101199)


**\[Text on screen\]**


Master Architect
Creating the ‘world’s best bank building’


**\[Norman\]**


If somebody wants to do the best of its kind, that has to be inspirational.


I mean, that has to be ‘wow, let's go for it.’


I think it encapsulated the spirit of this place and the idea that one could perhaps propose something that was so radical as a design, or something that would challenge the very essence of a tall building.


The big move was to take everything out of the heart of the space and to move it to one side to create the open loft spaces, to celebrate the views to the Peak, the views to the water, and uninterrupted lines of sight, good for communication, and to break it down into zones, so you had communal areas where people could communicate.


It also enabled the creation of a banking hall right in the centre of the space, and also lifting everything up so the pedestrians could flow under.


That has been a very enduring aspect of the project and is as alive and well today as it was on the drawing board.


The challenges were logistical, how you brought packaged elements from faraway places around the globe, brought them here, and then seamlessly integrated them.


I think that integration was an extraordinary combination of design and contracting challenges.


When you walk around a building site you realise that a building is man-made, all that equipment scooping the dirt, the mud, it's handcrafted where an army of people – and it seems like organised mayhem – finally ends up with something which is pristine, clean, inhabited that I think is still an extraordinary miracle and is a sense of wonderment still.


You can see the renderings, you can see the models, but nothing really prepares you for the real thing, the smell, the tactile qualities.


That's a very special moment.


This building set off a train of further explorations in terms of tall buildings.


It encouraged larger volumes to break up the mass of a building, to introduce nature into the buildings with an ecological, sustainable element.


But there is nothing like this building.


It is unique and special to its place.


It’s a positive gesture, a kind of beacon for the future, an optimistic belief in the future.


And that was really the brief of the bank, to do the best bank building in the world.


That was about Hong Kong, it was about the bank, it was about the community.


It was about a big idea.


And we all need big ideas.

**The brief was to create the best bank building in the world – that was about Hong Kong, it was about the bank, and about the community.**


The big move was to take everything out of the heart of the space and to move it to one side to create open loft spaces; to celebrate the views to the Peak and water and offer uninterrupted lines of sight – good for communication; and to break it down into zones so you had communal areas where people could communicate.


The challenges were logistical – how you brought packaged elements from faraway places around the globe, brought them here and then seamlessly integrated them. I remember us using many devices to anticipate and convey how it would look.


This building set off a train of further explorations in terms of tall buildings. It encouraged large volumes to break up the mass of a building and to introduce nature into the buildings with an ecological, sustainable element. These ideas were manifested in our more recent tall building designs.


## Forces of nature – from feng shui to typhoons – were woven into the engineering of the building


Early on, I was told that HSBC would take care of the site’s ‘feng shui’ – an aspect unfamiliar to me at the time. That immediately inspired me to speak with a feng shui expert. In the end, our design had the escalators on a line of axis that subliminally followed his advice.


I remember running seminars, involving external consultants that I brought in, to identify what the priorities of the bank were – in terms of space planning, efficiency, future image. I really want to underline the collaborative aspects of the project.


The lessons we learned by being here had to do with the importance of shading and using seawater cooling – in short, exploring emerging ideas of sustainability and flexibility. We also needed to account for future typhoons.


During construction, in 1983, we experienced Typhoon Ellen and had to angle the cranes into the line of the typhoon wind force to minimise wind resistance.
